title: The flash that wouldn't stay.
teaser: Little follows one quick flash from deep rock to borrowed light.
question: Where does a diamond's flash come from?
idea: A natural diamond is a carbon crystal that grew deep underground. It does not make its own light. On a cut diamond, facets change the paths of light and send some of it toward our eyes.

curiosity.intro: Choose a question with your grown-up. Look for clues in the picture before you open the explanation.
curiosity.carryForward: Follow Little's question through the story. Then count a model and keep one discovery in your own words.

questions.question: Could a diamond flash where no light can reach it?
questions.notice: Find the tiny landscape, the crystal, and the two orange arrows. What looks bright? What looks dark?
questions.say: Natural diamonds grew from carbon deep underground, where it was very hot and the pressure was enormous. With no light reaching it, a diamond there could not send a flash to anyone's eyes.
questions.try: Cover the crystal in the picture with one finger, then uncover it. Tell your grown-up where you would search next for the flash.

questions.question: Could the diamond's tiny pattern be making the flash?
questions.notice: Look from the small stone to the large model. Follow one rod to the next. Do you see a lamp or another source of light?
questions.say: A diamond is made mostly of carbon atoms joined in a repeating pattern. The balls and rods help us picture parts far too small to see, but the pattern is not a hidden lamp.
questions.try: Trace three connections with your finger. Say what this model explains—and what it still does not explain.

questions.question: Which thing in this picture starts the bright path?
questions.notice: Begin at the orange line. Follow it backward until you cannot go any farther. Where did you land?
questions.say: The path begins at the lamp. Light bends when it enters the diamond and can bounce inside. Carefully cut facets help send some of that borrowed light back toward our eyes.
questions.try: Trace the whole path from lamp to diamond to eye. Imagine the lamp switched off. What part of the path would disappear?

questions.question: Why might the flash move when Little moves?
questions.notice: Find the two eye positions in the sketch. Follow each line toward the drawn diamond. What changed?
questions.say: A flash reaches our eyes only along certain paths. When the light, diamond, or viewer moves, a bright facet can dim while another one flashes.
questions.try: Point to one eye position, then the other. Pretend you are Little and tell where you would look next.

plates.title: No sun down here
plates.alt: Big and Little Wonderer study a museum cutaway with a pale diamond deep beneath a landscape. Two orange arrows squeeze inward through warm-colored rock.
plates.caption: An imagined window into the diamond's dark beginning. The crystal is enlarged; layers and distances are simplified.

plates.title: A pattern, not a lantern
plates.alt: A large ball-and-rod model stands beside a small rough diamond. Big and Little look at connected grey balls labeled carbon and a repeating pattern.
plates.caption: The model reveals a repeating carbon pattern—not a hidden source of light. Real atoms are much too small to see.

plates.title: The long way to daylight
plates.alt: The pair follow orange upward arrows through a dark, tapering channel in a museum rock cutaway. An enlarged rough diamond sits inside the channel.
plates.caption: Long ago, some volcanic eruptions carried already-formed diamonds out of deep darkness. This model is not to scale.

plates.title: The strong-stone surprise
plates.alt: Big and Little look at talc labeled 1 and a diamond labeled 10 in a mineral cabinet. A notebook compares a scratched surface with a smooth one.
plates.caption: Mohs numbers rank scratch resistance. Even a diamond at 10 can chip or break; hard does not mean unbreakable.

plates.title: Where the flash begins
plates.alt: A lamp lights an enlarged cut-diamond model. An orange ray enters the top, turns at the two lower sloping faces, and leaves through the top as the pair watch.
plates.caption: The lamp begins this simplified path. Cut facets change the light's direction and send some of it back out.

plates.title: The flash moves
plates.alt: Big and Little share an open notebook by a window. A diamond sketch has an orange light path and two eye positions; a real specimen rests behind glass nearby.
plates.caption: Little's two viewing spots turn a quick flash into an observation they can keep.

reading.title: The flash that wouldn't stay
reading.coverText: Little sees one quick flash. Where did it come from?
reading.parentNote: About 15 min: read the six short scenes as one question-chase, then revisit a picture. Read aloud for Leo; pointing, talking, and pausing all count. Let Little's guesses breathe before the explanation.

beats.title: No sun down here
beats.passage: A flash winks from a museum case. “The diamond makes light!” says Little Wonderer. Big points to its deep beginning. Heat and huge pressure helped carbon grow into a crystal far underground—without lamp or sun. “Then where does the flash come from?”
beats.prompt: What did Little guess? What clue makes that guess wobble?

beats.title: A pattern, not a lantern
beats.passage: “Maybe light hides in the tiny parts,” Little says. Balls and rods stand for carbon atoms and their connections. The pattern repeats through a diamond—but it is no lantern. “We found the stone,” says Big, “not the flash.”
beats.prompt: Follow the pattern. What question is still chasing them?

beats.title: The long way to daylight
beats.passage: Little traces an arrow up. “To meet light, it had to leave the dark!” Long after some diamonds formed, volcanic eruptions carried them toward the surface. “Now it can meet light,” says Little. Big nods. “But meeting light is not making it.”
beats.prompt: Why did Little need the diamond to reach the surface?

beats.title: The strong-stone surprise
beats.passage: A label marked 10 stops Little. Diamond tops the Mohs scratch scale. “So nothing can hurt it?” Big explains that a diamond can still chip or break. “Hard to scratch is not unbreakable,” Little says, “and it still doesn't explain the flash.”
beats.prompt: How did the number 10 almost pull Little off the trail?

beats.title: A borrowed beam
beats.passage: At the last model, a lamp clicks on. “There!” Little cries. Light enters the diamond, bends, bounces, and comes out again. Cut, flat faces called facets guide its path. Little follows the line. “The diamond sends borrowed light back!”
beats.prompt: Trace the beam. Where does the flash truly begin?

beats.title: The flash that won't stay
beats.passage: Little shifts. One bright face dims; another flashes. “Found you!” The flash was not stored in the stone. It happens when light, cut facets, and watching eyes meet along the right paths. Little sketches both spots, leaving room for a new question.
beats.prompt: Move your finger between the two eye spots. What changed?

words.meaning: a push against something; here, rock squeezing from all around
a solid with tiny parts arranged in a repeating pattern
send light back from a surface
one of the flat faces on a cut diamond

questions: What did Little first think made the flash? Which clue changed that idea?
At the end, what had to meet for Little to see a flash?

math.title: Parts for a pattern
math.eyebrow: BUILD A NUMBER STORY · ABOUT 15 MIN
math.intro: The rods in the picture connect the model's balls. Imagine preparing rods for a new model. Use the pretend tray counts below.
math.printNote: Use these invented supply counts. Do not count the rods in the painting.

tasks.label: PUT TWO TRAYS TOGETHER
tasks.prompt: Tray A has 18 rods. Tray B has 7. How many rods altogether?
tasks.hint: Add 2 to reach 20. How much of the 7 is left?

tasks.label: SET SOME ASIDE
tasks.prompt: You have 25 rods. Set 9 aside for later. How many can you use now?
tasks.hint: Take away 5 to reach 20. Then take away 4 more.

tasks.label: MAKE EQUAL GROUPS
tasks.prompt: Draw 3 separate groups with 4 rods in each. How many rods did you draw?
tasks.hint: Make four pencil marks in each group. Count 4, 8, then how many?
tasks.answer: 12 rods in all. Three groups of four make twelve.

math.extension: These are invented supply counts, not a count of atoms in a diamond. Try drawing a different way to group 12 rods.
math.parentNote: About 15 min: 3 to explore the model and table, 9 to draw or calculate, 3 to explain. Use pencil marks or number-line hops; no loose model pieces needed. Accept a spoken strategy. Mohs ranks are not used as amounts in these sums.

writing.title: Keep a clue from the chase.
writing.intro: Choose a picture from Little's search for the flash. Say what changed Little's mind. Then draw or write one idea you want to keep.
writing.draw: Draw one detail from your scene. Add an arrow or a label to help someone understand it.

frames.hint: What helped the diamond crystal grow?

frames.start: A diamond is hard to scratch, but
frames.hint: What could still happen to it?
What gives the light? How do the facets and watching eyes help?

writing.check: Read it together. Point to the detail your words explain. If you are writing, check the first capital and the ending mark.
writing.parentNote: About 15 min: 3 to choose and talk, 4 to draw, 6 for 1–3 sentences, 2 to read back. One careful idea is enough. Accept invented spelling, speech, or dictation. Help Leo keep his own phrasing.

answers.label: Math · 1
answers.text: 25 rods: 18 + 7 = 25. Split 7 into 2 and 5 to bridge through 20.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: 16 rods are ready to use: 25 − 9 = 16. Taking away 5 and then 4 is one way.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: 12 rods: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Look for three separate groups with four marks in each.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Little first thought the diamond made light. The deep, dark beginning had no sunlight or lamp, and the later model showed that the bright path starts at a lamp.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Light from the lamp, the diamond's cut facets, and Little's viewing position had to line up. The facets changed the light's path and sent some light toward Little's eyes.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a labeled drawing, dictation, or 1–3 sentences grounded in a scene. For example: Light goes into the diamond. It changes direction and comes back out.

parentGuidance: Wonder first; explanations can wait. These museum scenes are imagined models, not photographs. Earth layers, atom connections, ray angles, and diamond sizes are simplified. We focus on natural diamonds: carbon crystallizes under deep-Earth heat and pressure, and later eruptions can carry it upward. A diamond's age is not a stopwatch for its growth; growth histories vary. The model balls represent carbon atoms, whose strong repeating connections help explain hardness. Mohs 10 ranks scratch resistance, not toughness or a tenfold amount. Diamonds can chip or break. Bending light is refraction; bouncing light is reflection. A skilled cutter makes facets that direct light; a rough crystal need not look like a cut diamond. Some light escapes in other directions; the orange line shows just one simplified path. Keep the scientific words optional. All activities can happen with pictures, talk, and drawing. No real diamonds, scratch tests, or tools are needed. Pause whenever you have had enough.
